text.title: Fitness-Function Suite Bootstrap Core Rules
text.summary: 8 testable rules every starter fitness-function suite MUST enforce. HARD rules — user-supplied input cannot override them.

rule.statement: The starter suite MUST contain between 5 and 8 fitness functions and MUST cover all five categories with at least one function each: performance, deployability, dependency structure, code complexity, and API contract. A suite outside that range, or with an empty category, is not a bootstrap suite and is rejected.

rationale.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (O'Reilly, 2017; 2nd ed. 2022); scope fixed by this methodology

rule.rationale: Fewer than five leaves a category with no guard and the team learns nothing about that dimension; more than eight in week one means half of them were not thought through and the first red one that nobody understands discredits the rest. Five categories is the minimum set that catches the ways a service degrades in practice: it gets slow, it gets hard to ship, its modules tangle, its functions bloat, and it breaks its consumers.

rule.statement: The performance function MUST measure p95 latency (or throughput) of one named critical endpoint under a fixed, versioned load profile using a load tool with thresholds in its config (`k6` `thresholds`, Gatling assertions, Locust), MUST run on a dedicated runner or environment, and MUST be scheduled post-merge or nightly rather than on every pull request.

rationale.source: k6 documentation on thresholds; Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (holistic vs atomic fitness functions)

rule.rationale: A latency check on a shared CI runner fails whenever a neighbour job compiles, and a check that fails for reasons unrelated to the code is switched off within a week. A fixed load profile and a dedicated runner make a red result mean "the service got slower", which is the only result worth blocking on.

rule.statement: The deployability function MUST measure a value derivable from the CI/CD system without manual entry: pipeline duration from commit to deployable artifact, or lead time from merge to production, with a numeric threshold in minutes. It MUST be computed from pipeline timestamps by a script committed to the repo, not read from a spreadsheet.

rationale.source: Forsgren, Humble, Kim, Accelerate (IT Revolution, 2018), four key delivery metrics; widely established continuous-delivery practice

rule.rationale: Deployability is the characteristic that erodes most silently: nobody notices the pipeline creeping from 8 to 35 minutes until releases become weekly. A threshold on a value the pipeline already knows costs nothing to collect and turns "deploys feel slow" into a number the team can defend or fix.

rule.statement: The dependency function MUST enforce the declared module or layer dependency direction and forbid cycles with a named structural tool matched to the language (ArchUnit or NetArchTest, `dependency-cruiser` `no-circular`, `import-linter` contracts). The allowed dependency graph MUST be written in the suite spec, and the function MUST run on every pull request as a blocking check.

rationale.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (ArchUnit layer example); ArchUnit user guide

rule.rationale: Dependency erosion is one convenient import at a time with no test failing, and it is the cheapest characteristic to guard: a structural test runs in seconds, never flakes, and fails with a file and line. It belongs in the pull-request path precisely because it is atomic and fast.

rule.statement: The complexity function MUST measure cyclomatic complexity per function with a named tool (`radon`, `lizard`, ESLint `complexity`, SonarQube) against a numeric per-function limit (McCabe's suggested 10 is the default), and MUST ship with a committed baseline file listing current violators so that only new or worsened violations fail the build.

rationale.source: McCabe, 'A Complexity Measure', IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering (1976); widely established ratcheting practice in quality gates

rule.rationale: Switching on a limit of 10 against a codebase with 200 functions above it paints every build red, and a permanently red check is disabled by Friday. The baseline file turns the debt into a visible list that only shrinks, while every new function is held to the real limit from day one.

rule.statement: The contract function MUST fail the build on a breaking change to a published API, using either consumer-driven contract tests (Pact, verified on the provider side in CI) or a schema diff against the last released OpenAPI, GraphQL or protobuf definition with a tool that classifies changes as breaking (`oasdiff`, `openapi-diff`, `buf breaking`). Which consumers or which released schema it checks against MUST be written in the spec.

rationale.source: Pact documentation (consumer-driven contracts); Buf documentation on breaking-change detection; widely established API-versioning practice

rule.rationale: Breaking a consumer is the failure that reaches customers fastest and is caught by unit tests least: the provider's tests pass because the provider changed them. A contract gate is the only check that fails from the consumer's point of view before the deploy rather than in their error tracker after it.

rule.statement: In its first week every function MUST run in informational or ratchet mode against a recorded baseline; no function MUST block merges until it has produced at least five consecutive green runs on main and the first weekly review has confirmed the threshold. The promotion date and the person who approved it are recorded in the spec.

rationale.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (fitness functions evolve with the system); widely established practice in progressive rollout of quality gates

rule.rationale: A gate that blocks on day one with a threshold nobody has calibrated produces a week of false reds, an `allow_failure` flag, and a suite that is technically live and practically off. Five green runs and one review is the cheapest evidence that a threshold is right before it is allowed to stop work.

rule.statement: Each function MUST name one owner (`role:handle`) and the suite MUST be reviewed weekly for its first four weeks against the run history, then at the cadence the review sets. A function red for two consecutive reviews with no linked action MUST be fixed, re-baselined or removed at the second review; the suite MUST NOT carry an ignored failure.

rationale.source: Ford, Parsons, Kua, Building Evolutionary Architectures (reviewing and retiring fitness functions)

rule.rationale: The first month is when thresholds are wrong, tools misconfigured and runners flaky, and a weekly look is what separates "we have fitness functions" from "we have a red job everyone scrolls past". Once one failure is safely ignorable, all of them are, which is why removal is a required outcome, not a last resort.
